name: setting-row
description:
One setting: what it is, what it does, and the control that changes it. The app has these across four settings pages — Account, Billing, Hosting and the index — each rebuilt from a flex row, a label, a description and a control, at four slightly different spacings.

The shape it enforces is the one that keeps a settings page readable: the description belongs UNDER the label and not beside the control, so the control column stays a straight edge down the page. A row where the control's position depends on how long the description is turns a settings page into a ragged list.

base.$description:
CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.

description.$description: Under the label, never beside the control. A row whose control position depends on the description's length turns a settings page into a ragged list — and the control column being a straight edge is what makes the page scannable.

layout.$description: On a phone the control drops below the copy rather than squeezing beside it — a toggle at the end of a 40-character row is a target nobody can hit.

danger.$description: A destructive setting — delete the account, revoke everything. The row is tinted so it is visibly not one of the others, and the control inside it wears the danger variant.

a11y.note: The description is tied to the control with `aria-describedby`, or it is decoration a screen-reader user never hears — which matters most on exactly the rows where the description says what will be lost. A destructive row is not marked by tint alone: its control says what it does in words, and the confirm dialog wears the same danger variant as the trigger.
